pl-l2d33c5-d1e108.summary: States that though infants are bound only by Adam's sin among parental sins, parents' sins do redound on children: God says he visits fathers' iniquities on children to the third and fourth generation of those who hate him.

pl-l2d33c5-d1e113.summary: Notes the apparent conflict with Ezekiel 18: no longer shall the proverb be used, 'the fathers ate sour grapes and the children's teeth are set on edge'; the soul that sins shall die; the son shall not bear the father's iniquity.
claims: Ezekiel denies the son bears the father's guilt.

pl-l2d33c5-d1e116.summary: States that God seems to correct through the prophet what he said badly in the Law; for if he renders fathers' sins to later generations, it seems unjust that one sins and another is punished.

pl-l2d33c5-d1e120.summary: Cites Jerome: lest the Law and the Prophets, indeed God, seem to disagree, note the end of the Exodus text, 'of those who hate me,' showing that children are punished not because their fathers sinned but because they, like them, hate God by a hereditary evil.
claims: Children are punished for their own hatred of God.

pl-l2d33c5-d1e123.summary: Explains, with Jerome on Ezekiel and Augustine on the Psalm, that the Exodus text concerns children who imitate their fathers' sins and are punished for that imitation; God does not correct in the prophet what he said in the Law but shows how to understand it, rebuking those who misread it with the proverb.
claims: Ezekiel explains the Law, not corrects it.

pl-l2d33c5-d1e128.summary: Asks why, if it concerns imitators, only the third and fourth generation are mentioned, and why fathers, since all who imitate anyone's sins are evil.

pl-l2d33c5-d1e131.summary: Answers that fathers are named because children chiefly imitate fathers, whom they love most; and the third and fourth generation because parents sometimes live to see such descendants, who, seeing their iniquities, become heirs of their impiety by imitation. So the literal sense is right.
claims: Parents may live to see four generations.

pl-l2d33c5-d1e134.summary: Gives the mystical sense, since it is called a parable: the father is the first light prick of sense, the first motion of suggestion or thought; the son, when thought conceives sin, the woman's consent and delight; the grandson, when what is conceived is done or decided upon, the man's consent; the great-grandson, when one glories in it. God does not eternally punish first and second stirrings of thought, called propatheiai, without which no human exists, but the decision to act and refusal to correct, which are mortal sins.
claims: First motions are not punished eternally.
Decision to sin and glorying in it are mortal.

pl-l2d33c5-d1e137.summary: Adds with Jerome that Genesis shows the first stirring of thought is not punished eternally: Ham sinned by mocking his father's nakedness, but his son Canaan received the curse; this was said in mystery, since it would be unjust otherwise.
claims: Canaan's curse is to be read mystically.

pl-l2d33c5.summary: Though infants are bound only by Adam's sin, parents' sins do redound on children: God visits the fathers' iniquities to the third and fourth generation (Exod 20:5). This seems to conflict with Ezekiel 18, where the son does not bear the father's iniquity, and with justice. With Jerome and Augustine, Lombard resolves it: Exodus adds 'of those who hate me,' so children are punished not because their fathers sinned but because they imitate them; Ezekiel explains rather than corrects the Law. Fathers are named because children chiefly imitate them, and the third and fourth generations because parents may live to see them. Mystically, the four generations are the first motion of thought, the conceiving of sin, its completion or decision, and glorying in it; God does not eternally punish the first motions (propatheiai) but the decision and refusal to correct. So Canaan was cursed for Ham's sin in mystery.
claims: Infants are bound only by Adam's sin, yet parents' sins redound on children.
Exodus and Ezekiel do not conflict.
Children are punished for imitating their fathers' sins, not for their fathers' sins as such.
Fathers are named because children imitate them most.
Mystically, the four generations are stages of sin from first motion to glorying in it.
First motions of thought are not punished eternally; decision and refusal to correct are mortal.
